transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2026-09-16
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Malik (Redwood AE); Tom Chen (Redwood SE); Priya Rao (Redwood CSM); Lena Ortiz (ArborPay Eng Mgr); Marcus Lee (ArborPay SRE); Nina Patel (ArborPay Head Product)

Summary:
Quick rehearsal of the staging->prod switchover playbook. Re-validate canary thresholds, monitoring hooks, rollback criteria, KMS keyflow, and compliance checklist. Agree next steps and owners for a dry-run next week.

Topics:
- Canary thresholds and SLO gates
- Traffic gating and AB variants
- Monitoring & alert ownership (telemetry handoff)
- Runbook dry-run schedule and responsibilities
- Security: KMS, audit logs, SOC2 questions

Action Items (from this call):
- Tom: update runbook with explicit canary thresholds and signal definitions (due 2026-09-20)
- Marcus: provision traffic replay in staging and attach dataset (due 2026-09-21)
- Aisha: send dedicated pricing delta + pilot SLA options (due 2026-09-18)
- Nina: collect compliance questionnaire answers for KMS/HSM (due 2026-09-24)

Transcript:
[00:00] Aisha Malik: Hey everyone? Thanks for making time. Quick check—do we have everyone on the line?
[00:05] Lena Ortiz: Yep, Lena here. Marcus is on as well. Nina joined a little late but she's here.
[00:10] Marcus Lee: Hey, sorry for the hop in, been heads down on the replay infra. Good to be here.
[00:14] Tom Chen: Tom from Redwood — we'll be walking through the switchover steps and the canary gating.
[00:20] Priya Rao: Priya here, I'll be watching action item assignment and follow up.

[02:05] Aisha Malik: Alright, goal for today is a dry rehearsal of the playbook — we don't need to run traffic, but we need the decision points, the telemetry checks, and the rollback paths to be explicit. Marcus, can you remind us of staging parity with prod? any gaps?
[02:22] Marcus Lee: Staging mirrors prod for the most part; CPU/GPU resource limits are slightly lower — we have same model versions and quantization, but the network egress patterns differ. One caveat: our KMS staging key is a separate key and we don't have HSM test hooks. So any KMS rotation path hasn't been exercised end-to-end.
[02:45] Nina Patel: For compliance we need to show the key flow and audit log samples. SOC two? I mean, SOC 2, sorry, we have the template but need the redwood audit log format.
[02:58] Tom Chen: We can export audit logs — there's an endpoint. We also have an example doc. I'll drop the link in chat after the call. Note, the KMS integration for private deploys uses customer-managed keys if you pick Private; for Dedicated it's optional.

[05:10] Aisha Malik: Let's step through the playbook. Step one — traffic gating config. Step two — smoke tests. Step three — canary ramp. Step four — full cutover. Step five — verification and rollback window. I'll read the first two bullets and Tom you can annotate.
[05:28] Tom Chen: Sounds good. For traffic gating: we suggest starting at 1% traffic for 15 minutes, watch latency p50/p95, error rate, AI hallucination rate from our eval hooks, and compare to baseline. If any SLO breaches occur, auto-abort and roll back. For smoke tests: synthetic prompts across top 10 intents.
[06:05] Lena Ortiz: The 1% feels conservative; our business wants faster ramp. Could we do 5% with a shorter observation window?
[06:12] Tom Chen: You could, but risk increases. The runtime has continuous batching which can amplify latency under bursty spikes — that was part of the reason we kept it low. Also note quantization differences will show up in token-level latencies.
[06:30] Marcus Lee: Another constraint — our customer-facing SLA requires sub-200ms median on one of the endpoints. In staging we're at ~220ms median on long prompts. If we ramp faster we might breach your SLOs in real traffic.

[08:00] Nina Patel: Can we set different thresholds per route? We have one high-volume route and a couple infrequent ones.
[08:07] Tom Chen: Yes — runbook supports per-route thresholds and canary profiles. We'll define baseline and tolerance per route. I'll add the matrix.

[10:20] Aisha Malik: Ok, canary thresholds—what signals should be gating? List them out.
[10:27] Tom Chen: Primary signals: p95 latency, error rate (5xx), model-specific quality regression (we'll run prompt set evals and compare likelihoods/metrics), and user-visible failure rate. Secondary signals: CPU/GPU memory pressure, token throughput, KV cache hit rate.
[11:00] Marcus Lee: For quality regression — what's the mechanism? Is it offline eval or realtime sampling?
[11:05] Tom Chen: Both. We recommend a small live sample of user requests forwarded to a shadow instance and an offline evaluation run on saved prompts that we compare to baseline. If the regression metric exceeds 2% relative drop, trigger rollback.
[11:30] Lena Ortiz: Got it. That 2% threshold — can we make it 3%? Our product team is a bit more tolerant.
[11:35] Nina Patel: We prefer to balance user impact but also not be blind to regressions. Maybe agree per-route tolerance.
[11:42] Priya Rao: I'll capture per-route tolerance as an action item.

[14:00] Aisha Malik: Next, monitoring and ownership — who owns which alerts during the window?
[14:07] Marcus Lee: ArborPay SRE will own infra and latency alerts; Redwood will own model quality alerts and fallback triggers. We need an on-call handoff plan for the three-hour safety window, and exact pager contacts.
[14:30] Tom Chen: Redwood can own the first responder for model-side anomalies; we'll escalate to ArborPay SRE for infra issues. We'll put contacts in the runbook.
[15:05] Nina Patel: Please include run escalation steps and exact Slack channels. We need an audit trail.

[17:00] Aisha Malik: On rollback criteria — we mentioned auto-abort on SLO breach. Do you want auto-rollback to previous model or immediate traffic diversion to a simpler endpoint (e.g., cached responses)?
[17:15] Marcus Lee: Immediate traffic diversion to a cached fallback adds complexity but reduces customer impact. Might be worth it for payments-critical flows.
[17:28] Tom Chen: Our platform supports a fallback router to a 'safe' model variant or cached responses. Fallback config is in the traffic-policy section of the runbook.
[17:40] Lena Ortiz: How fast is a rollback? We're thinking under 2 minutes to revert routing.
[17:45] Tom Chen: If the automation triggers, it's sub-30 seconds for routing change; full model instance drain can take a couple of minutes. You should expect a 1–3 minute window where some requests might hit in-flight instances.

[20:00] Aisha Malik: Let's drill into the AB experiment option — we talked about A/B for ranking model variants earlier.
[20:06] Tom Chen: For AB we recommend traffic slicing by user-id hash, keep 50/50 for evaluation or 90/10 for canaries. Use the telemetry hooks to compare engagement and error signals. Keep the experiment duration at least 24 hours for signal stability.
[20:40] Nina Patel: 24 hours sounds long. For a quick check could we do 6 hours if the signals are clean?
[20:46] Tom Chen: You can, but small sample sizes will increase noise; our heuristics will reflect that.

[22:30] Marcus Lee: About the staging dry-run — I want to run a replay from the last 48 hours of traffic to simulate production patterns. Redwood, do you have tooling for traffic replay or should we use our infra?
[22:42] Tom Chen: We have a replay harness and recommend using your staging replay. We can provide a replay adapter to map headers and tokens. Marcus, if you share the dataset we'll help run it.
[23:05] Marcus Lee: OK I'll provision and send credentials.

[24:40] Aisha Malik: Security items: KMS and audit logs. Nina, you said you need artifacts. We'll include a sample audit log export and a KMS flow diagram.
[24:50] Tom Chen: Note: in Private deploys, KMS is customer-managed; be careful with key rotation during switchover. We can coordinate a freeze window.
[25:05] Nina Patel: We want to ensure rotation won't break token decryption during the cutover.
[25:12] Tom Chen: Agreed. We'll add a pre-cutover KMS validation step in the runbook — verify decrypt/encrypt on a sample payload.

[28:00] Aisha Malik: Now runbook specifics — Tom, can you call out the sequence numbers and expected durations? We need these in the rehearsal deck.
[28:10] Tom Chen: Sure. Sequence: 1) Preflight checks (10–15m) — infra, KMS, metrics baseline. 2) Smoke tests (5–10m) — synthetic prompts. 3) Canary start (1% for 15m). Monitor. 4) Canary ramp (1%→5%→20% over 45–90m depending on signals). 5) Final cutover (5–10m). 6) Post-cut checks (30–60m observation).
[28:40] Marcus Lee: For our hours-of-operation we'll need to align the final cutover to a quiet window — likely Saturday night.
[28:48] Aisha Malik: We'll note that. Also, re: duration, we'll include auto gates with the option to skip manual approval if all signals are green and a trusted operator token is present.

[31:20] Lena Ortiz: One more question — telemetry retention and access. After cutover, how long are detailed traces available? We sometimes need 90 days for investigations.
[31:30] Tom Chen: Default is 30 days in hosted; enterprise plans can extend to 90/365 days. For Dedicated we can arrange a retention plan. We'll surface pricing delta.
[31:45] Aisha Malik: Action: Aisha to share retention options and cost.

[33:50] Nina Patel: Are there known edge cases from other pilots you can call out? Anything we should watch for that might not be obvious?
[33:58] Tom Chen: One we've seen: KV cache warm-up causing a transient spike in latency on ramp. To mitigate, pre-warm caches with top-n prefixes or seed KV from a backup during preflight. Also watch for tokenization variance when switching model variants — prompt truncation differences can change outputs.
[34:25] Marcus Lee: Noted. We'll add pre-warm step.

[36:10] Aisha Malik: Ok, final section — dry-run schedule. Marcus, can you propose a date?
[36:16] Marcus Lee: Can we do 2026-09-22 at 02:00 UTC? That gives us time to prepare.
[36:23] Nina Patel: That window works for product. I'll be on-call for compliance checks.
[36:30] Tom Chen: Redwood can join for the dry-run and assist with telemetry dashboards. We'll bring the canary gating config and the rollback script.

[38:00] Aisha Malik: Great. Any other items? Competitor check—are you also evaluating smaller managed vendors?
[38:07] Lena Ortiz: We're also running a short eval with one of the cloud vendors just to compare latency and cost, but Redwood's per-route controls are the reason we're leaning here.
[38:20] Nina Patel: We're watching price and SLA; also looking at Bedrock's integration.
[38:27] Tom Chen: Understood.

[40:10] Priya Rao: I'll recap the next steps and owners: Tom updates runbook (due 9/20), Marcus provisions replay and sends dataset (9/21), Aisha sends pricing delta and retention options (9/18), Nina completes compliance artifacts (9/24). Marcus to confirm dry-run on 9/22.

[41:30] Marcus Lee: Quick technical note — for the traffic replay we need a mapping table for user IDs so experiments don't leak identifiers. We'll anonymize but need consistent hashing.
[41:45] Tom Chen: We can add a mapper; agree on consistent salt for hashing.

[44:00] Aisha Malik: Okay, thanks everyone. We'll share the updated runbook and a rehearsal checklist after this call. Tom, can you drop the audit log example and the runbook link in the notes?
[44:14] Tom Chen: Yep I'll paste links. Link: https://redwood.app/runbooks/arborpay-switchover-v1. Link: https://redwood.app/audit-exports/sample-auditlog-2026-08.json
[44:30] Nina Patel: Thanks, that helps.
[44:40] Lena Ortiz: Thanks all. See you at the dry-run.
[47:00] Aisha Malik: End of call — good rehearsal. We'll follow up in email and update CRM.

End Transcript
